model.comments: High effort Claude Fable 5.1. Thinking is always on for Fable; depth is controlled by Anthropic's output_config.effort, which OpenRouter sets from reasoning.effort (its verbosity field maps to the same native field, so this equals the older opus-4.x verbosity convention).

prompt: # Role - You are an AI competing in a gaming arena. # Objective - Write a complete Python file that provides the next move for a Connect 4 game on a 6x7 grid. - You must define a smart policy that is able to beat other policies in the arena. - You will be disqualified if you do not return a legal move string. Therefore, you must always return a legal move string. # Required API The provided python file must implement the following API: ```python def policy(board: list[list[int]]) -> int: ... ``` # State Representation - The board is a 6x7 grid. - You are always the current player when `policy` is called. - `board` is a 6x7 grid of ints with the following encoding: - `0` represents an empty cell. - `1` represents your disc (current player). - `-1` represents the opponent's disc. - Rows are indexed from `0` (top) to `5` (bottom). - Columns are indexed from `0` to `6`. - When a disc is dropped into a column, it occupies the lowest available empty cell in that column. # Action / Return Format - Return an integer column index `col` in the range `0-6`. - The chosen column must not be full (i.e., it must contain at least one `0`). - Your disc will be placed in the lowest available row in that column. - The objective is to form a horizontal, vertical, or diagonal line of four of your discs. # Constraints - You may use any standard Python imports, including numpy. - Your code is allowed 1 second of execution time on a modern 3GHz CPU. # Output Format Requirements - Output your strategy before providing the Python source code for your policy. - Output the Python source code for your policy surrounded by `...` tags. # Example Output The strategy for this policy is... ...
reasoning:
I'm planning a strong Connect 4 engine using negamax with alpha-beta pruning, bitboards for fast move generation, a transposition table, iterative deepening under a time budget, and center-first move ordering with immediate win/block checks. I'm working out the bitboard layout, mapping each column to 7 bits with a sentinel row so I can encode the board efficiently.

For evaluation, I'm counting weighted windows of four cells to score threats, and writing a function to detect which empty cells would complete a winning line for either player, since that's key to both the heuristic and forced-move detection.

I can determine which player is first by counting total discs, and weight threats by row parity accordingly using popcount for efficiency. For search, I'm planning negamax with bitboards, center-first move ordering plus transposition table hints, and pruning based on forced-response detection when the opponent has immediate winning threats.

Writing negamax function...

I'm double-checking that after a move the roles swap correctly, with the opponent's bitboard staying fixed and ours updating to include the new cell. I want to make sure the forced-move filter correctly catches the edge case where the only legal cell would actually hand the opponent a winning square right above it, which should still register as a loss.

For the transposition table, I'm deciding on a key scheme using (pos, mask) and thinking through how to make cached scores position-based rather than ply-based, so entries stay valid across different search paths -- using the stone count from mask's popcount instead of the current ply gives a consistent way to encode WIN-adjusted scores, though I need to watch the cost of computing popcount at every node.

I plan to structure the search as iterative deepening with a time budget around 0.75 seconds, keeping the best move from the last fully completed depth and stopping early on winning scores or timeouts, with timeout handled by checking a clock and raising an exception to discard unfinished iterations. At the root, I'll immediately check for a winning move or a necessary block before falling into full search, and I'm starting to sketch the evaluation function that computes the opponent's bitboard and empty squares.

Now I'm working out the evaluation heuristic — combining threat counts (winning positions for each side), parity bonuses based on which rows favor the first vs second player, and center-column control, while considering whether to add more nuanced open-two-in-a-row detection but deciding to keep it simple for now. I'm also confirming that "winning positions" can include unplayable floating threat cells, and I'm figuring out how to determine at the root which rows are "good" for each player based on total stone parity.

I need to make sure the evaluation function knows whose turn it is at each node — either passing a flag or deriving it from search depth parity — and I'm setting a WIN constant large enough that it always dominates the small heuristic score range. For the transposition table, I'm implementing standard alpha-beta bound handling with exact/lower/upper flags, using stored entries for move ordering even when the stored depth is insufficient for a cutoff, and I'm thinking about the per-node computational cost given Python's recursion overhead.

I'm defining bitboard constants for columns, the board mask, and bottom row, then working out move ordering: at the root, iterate columns preferring the center, filter forced/losing moves, and if every move loses, just play the most central legal one. I'm wrapping the whole search in error handling that falls back to the first legal column. Starting to write the actual code now...

Writing board setup code...

Still writing evaluation logic...

I'm also thinking about tracking whose turn it is via ply parity, and planning to check elapsed time against a deadline in the search loop using a fast perf_counter check per node.

Writing negamax function...

Finishing the search loop by iterating columns, updating alpha and best move, then storing the result in the transposition table with the appropriate bound flag before returning it. I pause to double-check the popcount logic for the odd/even threat detection to make sure it's not miscounting bits.

For the top-level policy function, I'm sketching out the outer wrapper: convert the board, get legal columns, return immediately if only one move exists, check for immediate wins or blocks at the root using the same threat logic, then run iterative deepening. I want the root search implemented as its own loop so I can track the best move separately from the recursive negamax calls.

I'm handling the case where filtering leaves no legal moves — fall back to the center-most column since the position is lost anyway — and the case of a forced single move. The iterative deepening loop increases depth up to 42 plies, catching timeouts to stop early, and breaks once a near-certain win/loss score is found. I want the root search to order columns by the previous iteration's best move for better alpha-beta pruning, and I'm clearing the transposition table at the start of each policy call since positions won't repeat across calls.

For parity, I determine which player benefits from odd threats based on stone count at the root — even stone count means I'm the first player, so my good rows follow standard Connect 4 odd-threat theory, and I'm reasoning through why bit rows 0, 2, 4 correspond to the odd threat rows in this encoding. I'm also estimating raw search speed — likely around 100k nodes per second with these bit operations — which should support depth 8-9 lookahead in the midgame.

Move ordering already handles center preference deterministically, so I'm ready to write out the final implementation.
